title: The readings and the psalm
hook: Sundays run a three-year cycle so most of the Bible is read aloud

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gloria: the angels' song, grown into a hymn and silent in Advent and Lent. Your line was glory to God in the highest.

The Gloria ends, the priest says a short opening prayer, and everyone sits down. That's the signal. The first part of the Mass, the gathering, the mercy and the praise, is over. Now comes the second: listening. A person walks up to a stand called the ambo. Very often it isn't the priest. It's a parishioner, a teacher or a retired mailman or a nervous sixteen-year-old, reading from a big book to a room full of people. And the passage wasn't chosen by the priest that week, or by them. It was chosen decades ago, for this exact Sunday, by a plan that runs across three years.
screen: `EVERYONE SITS.` → `A PARISHIONER AT THE AMBO.` → `CHOSEN DECADES AGO.`

segments.voice: Lectionary comes from the Latin lectio, a reading. It's the book of readings for Mass, laid out day by day. At the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s, the bishops asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up much more richly to the people. So a new lectionary was built, in use from 1970. On a Sunday there are four readings, counting the psalm. First, usually from the Old Testament, chosen to echo the day's Gospel. Then a psalm, sung or said: a cantor sings the verses, and everyone answers with a short refrain. Then a reading from one of the apostles' letters, often Paul. Then the Gospel. The Sundays run in a three-year cycle. Year A reads mostly from Matthew. Year B, Mark. Year C, Luke. John comes in around the great seasons, Lent and Easter, and fills out the short year of Mark. So over three years, a Catholic who comes every week hears the Gospels in turn and a wide sweep of the rest of the Bible. Not every word, but far more than before the reform, when one year of readings repeated over and over. Weekdays have their own cycle. And on any given Sunday, Roman Rite parishes around the world, in many languages, are reading the same passages. At the end of each reading, the reader says, in the old Latin, Verbum Domini, the word of the Lord. And the people answer, Deo gratias, thanks be to God.
screen: `LECTIO: A READING.` · `FOUR READINGS ON A SUNDAY.` · `YEAR A, B, C.` · `THE SAME PASSAGES, WORLDWIDE.` · then, large: `THANKS BE TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Say it again in your head, slower, and notice which word catches: lamp, feet, paths. You don't have to decide what it means, just carry it for a minute; if you pray, you can let it become your prayer.
Lectionary. The book of readings for Mass, laid out so that over three years of Sundays, a wide sweep of the Bible is read aloud. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, in turns. Three years of Sundays, read aloud by ordinary voices. That's day one hundred and eight.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, lay readers usually proclaim the first and second readings from the ambo, a cantor leads the responsorial psalm, and the readings follow a three-year cycle (Years A, B and C) shared by Roman Rite parishes worldwide.

what a scholar hears: the Ordo Lectionum Missae of 1969, answering the Council's call in Sacrosanctum Concilium 51 to open the Bible's treasures more lavishly.

chat.says: Does the priest pick the Bible readings each Sunday?
options: No. A plan running over three years sets them, the same in parishes around the world.
Yes. Each priest chooses passages that fit what he wants to preach that week.
No. The reader picks a favorite passage the week before and practices it.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook fixed (the collect comes between the Gloria and sitting down); 'after the Council' corrected to 'at the Council' (Sacrosanctum Concilium 51 is the Council's own text); four readings now 'counting the psalm'; 'a large share of the Bible', 'hundreds of languages' and 'two-year' weekday cycle (true only of first readings) softened; 'Catholic churches worldwide' narrowed to Roman Rite parishes; 'the shortest Gospel' superlative cut; stock 'here's the lovely part' cut.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 118:105 given from memory; confirm.

The index hook says 'most of the Bible is read aloud' and the carry says 'the whole book'. Studies suggest the Sunday cycle covers a minority of the Old Testament and a large share of the Gospels; the script says 'a large share' and 'not every word'. A Keeper may want the index hook softened.
New lectionary promulgated 1969, in use from Advent 1969/1970; weekday first readings on a two-year cycle. Confirm.
Easter season first readings come from Acts rather than the Old Testament; the script says 'usually from the Old Testament'. Confirm.
'Verbum Domini / Deo gratias' Latin acclamations; English responses described, not quoted from ICEL ('Thanks be to God' is a traditional phrase).
